title: Clearing the Table: Setting Boundaries Around Food, Alcohol, and Table Talk
coreMove: A food or drink boundary holds best when your answer stays short and repeatable, with an exit ready instead of a debate over health, taste, or tradition.

exampleSpecs.audience: a person declining food while handling public paperwork
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether a declined dish becomes a public defense of 30 days of Whole30.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Two named people let a short food refusal stand without turning it into a nutrition debate.

exampleSpecs.audience: a guest declining alcohol during a social ritual
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether a repeated offer makes the drink refusal look like a judgment of the party.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Set up the expected awkwardness of refusing alcohol, then reveal the pressure loses steam when the no stays short.

exampleSpecs.audience: a student setting terms before a family meal
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether body comments and diet talk get stopped before dinner starts.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: A short message exchange lets the body-talk boundary land between the lines.

exampleSpecs.audience: a lead trying to stop diet talk during a routine count
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether a joke about bodies becomes part of the normal loading rhythm.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: A routine gets interrupted by body comments, then restarts with a clear table-talk rule.

exampleSpecs.domain: bike-share meetup before a rooftop party
exampleSpecs.audience: a person arriving with a nonalcoholic drink
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether a repeated offer gets to define party belonging.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: One small lived moment shows alcohol refusal without a decision speech.

exampleSpecs.audience: a person reviewing whether leaving the table was too much
exampleSpecs.stakes: Whether the exit is judged against the pressure that came before it.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Reconstruct the family-table pressure from evidence after the outcome is known.
